title: How Should England's Curriculum & Assessment Review Respond to AI?
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou argues that generative AI has already broken the basic assumptions underpinning England's assessment system, and that the government's ongoing curriculum and assessment review must respond directly rather than treat AI as a passing trend. She cites sharp increases in student AI use - UK university assessment use rising from 53% to 88% between 2024 and 2025, and 13-18 year-olds' use rising from 37% to 77% - combined with the fact that AI detectors are unreliable, meaning undetectable AI use now threatens the integrity of written assessment itself. Christodoulou sets out five concrete recommendations: review AI marking systems' agreement with human judgment, revise initial teacher training's assumptions about AI in assessment, eliminate non-examined written coursework, retain handwritten exams for their cognitive and anti-cheating benefits, and investigate post-qualification university admissions now that AI marking could speed up results. Her larger argument is paradoxical but pointed: solving the AI problem requires reverting to old-fashioned, analogue, in-person exam formats, even as new AI technology makes those older formats newly efficient to administer (for example, by transcribing handwritten scripts). She closes by insisting that the pre-AI narrative of screen-based, un-Googleable assessment is now obsolete and the system must adapt quickly.
points: Christodoulou's key statistic: UK university students' use of AI for assessments rose from 53% in 2024 to 88% in 2025, and 13-18 year-olds' generative AI use rose from 37% in 2023 to 77% in 2024
with AI detectors unable to reliably catch it.

Her central category-error argument: assessment isn't about the end product but about what that product reveals of the process the student went through, which is exactly what AI-generated work erases.

Her five concrete recommendations for the curriculum and assessment review: review AI marking systems, revise initial teacher training on AI and assessment, eliminate non-examined written coursework, keep handwritten exams, and investigate post-qualification university admissions.

The paradox she identifies: fixing the AI assessment crisis requires reverting to old-fashioned, analogue, handwritten, in-person exam formats - even as new AI tools (like automated transcription of handwritten scripts) make those old formats newly efficient.
Her stark framing of the stakes: in the worst-case scenario, 'we end up with a kabuki dance where students pretend to write essays and teachers pretend to mark them.'
quotes: In that short time, developments in generative AI have obliterated some of our basic assumptions about assessment.
In the UK, at university level, the number of students using AI for assessments went up from 53 per cent in 2024 to 88 per cent in 2025.
Not only that, but you can't spot its use: AI detectors don't work. They miss real plagiarism and accuse human work of being plagiarised.
In the worst-case scenario, which may already be here, we end up with a kabuki dance where students pretend to write essays and teachers pretend to mark them.
What matters in an assessment is not the end product; it's what the end product tells you about the process the student went through to get there.

There are important cognitive benefits to handwriting, and if students know the final assessment is handwritten it will make them more likely to practise using that format too, and less likely to use AI.
That world is gone and it's not coming back. We have to adapt, quickly.
